claims.text: The initial material is an as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy produced by casting or solidification.
The as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy contains multiple constituent phases.
Advanced free-energy sampling can map the free-energy landscape of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Metadynamics or refined phase-field modeling can predict phase-transformation free-energy barriers under different annealing conditions.
Free-energy predictions can guide tailored annealing treatments that controllably tune phase evolution and phase fractions in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
Changing annealing temperature can cause HEAs to decompose into multiple phases.
High-temperature annealing makes atomic diffusion significant enough to enable the predicted transformation kinetics.
Relative free-energy barriers govern the nucleation and growth of the different phases.
Phase decomposition in HEAs reflects an interplay between configurational entropy and the enthalpies of mixing.
Identifying favorable thermodynamic conditions permits annealing to selectively stabilize or suppress constituent phases.
Selective stabilization or suppression of phases drives predictable and controlled phase transformations in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs.
The proposed treatment can controllably increase or decrease FCC, BCC, or other phase fractions.
Tailoring phase fractions can produce a tailored microstructure.
A tailored multiphase microstructure may improve mechanical properties.
Conventional annealing produces less predictable microstructures because multi-principal-element systems have complex free-energy landscapes.
The method's effectiveness depends on the accuracy of free-energy predictions for complex alloys.
Heating rate, atmosphere, and diffusion kinetics can affect the experimentally realized phase evolution.
The quantitative relationship between predicted free-energy barriers and experimentally achieved phase fractions is uncertain.
X-ray diffraction can be used for phase identification and phase-distribution assessment.

Failure of prediction-guided annealing to produce a statistically significant phase-distribution difference from conventional annealing, or observation of evolution contrary to the prediction, would falsify the hypothesis.
